Now, let's move on to the proof that a step function f / [a, b] -> \mathbb{R} is Riemann Integrable.

A step function f is a function that can be written as a finite linear combination of indicator functions of intervals. In other words, f(x) = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i \mathbb{I}_{[a_i, b_i]}(x), where a_i, b_i are distinct points in [a, b] and c_i are constants.

To prove that f is Riemann Integrable, we need to show that the upper and lower Riemann sums converge to the same value as the partition of the interval [a, b] is refined.

Let P be a partition of [a, b] into n subintervals [x_{i-1}, x_i]. Let f_P be the step function obtained by evaluating f at the points x_i.

The upper Riemann sum U(P, f) is defined as:

U(P, f) = ∑_{i=1}^n M_i (x_i - x_{i-1})

where M_i = sup_{x \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]} f(x).

Similarly, the lower Riemann sum L(P, f) is defined as:

L(P, f) = ∑_{i=1}^n m_i (x_i - x_{i-1})

where m_i = inf_{x \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]} f(x).

Since f is a step function, we have:

M_i = f(x_i) and m_i = f(x_i)

Therefore, U(P, f) = ∑_{i=1}^n f(x_i) (x_i - x_{i-1}) and L(P, f) = ∑_{i=1}^n f(x_i) (x_i - x_{i-1})

As the partition P is refined, the intervals [x_{i-1}, x_i] become smaller, and the values of f(x_i) become closer together. This means that the upper and lower Riemann sums U(P, f) and L(P, f) converge to the same value, which is the definite integral of f over [a, b].

Therefore, we have shown that a step function f / [a, b] -> \mathbb{R} is Riemann Integrable.

Please note that this proof assumes that the function f is bounded and has at most a finite number of discontinuities. If f has an infinite number of discontinuities or is unbounded, the proof may not hold.
